```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# Figures for the section on the published series, read from the series file
# and from the comparison of every option of the full menu with its twins on
# the curve of the claim
series <- readr::read_csv("../cases/eu-frames/data/macro/predictor_measures.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(dplyr::between(year, 2004, 2013), !is.na(value))
curve <- readr::read_csv("../cases/eu-frames/data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
forks <- readr::read_csv("../cases/eu-frames/data/spec_curve_forks.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(curve == "positive")
devs <- readr::read_csv("../cases/eu-frames/data/menu_deviations.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(curve == "positive", axis == "measure")
tips <- datawizard::data_filter(devs, option == "es_1574_tips")
es_growth <- datawizard::data_filter(devs, option == "es_growth")
coverage <- series |>
  dplyr::summarise(cells = dplyr::n(), countries = dplyr::n_distinct(cntry), .by = measure)
unemp_curve <- datawizard::data_filter(curve, predictor == "unemp")

# Shares printed to one decimal, rounding halves up
measure_share <- sprintf("%.1f%%", floor(forks$share[forks$axis == "measure"] * 10 + 0.5) / 10)
tips_below <- sprintf("%.1f%%", floor(tips$below_zero_sig * 10 + 0.5) / 10)
tips_changes <- sprintf("%.1f%%", floor(tips$class_changes * 10 + 0.5) / 10)
curve_below <- sprintf("%.1f%%", floor(100 * mean(unemp_curve$supports & unemp_curve$sig) * 10 + 0.5) / 10)

# The four full-coverage unemployment series, with the means of each country and
# of each year removed (sequential demeaning is exact on a balanced panel)
full <- c("wb_nat", "es_1574_act", "es_2064_pop", "es_2564_lfs")
within_cor <- series |>
  datawizard::data_filter(measure %in% full) |>
  dplyr::mutate(value = value - mean(value), .by = c(measure, cntry)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(value = value - mean(value), .by = c(measure, year)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(id_cols = c(cntry, year), names_from = measure, values_from = value) |>
  dplyr::select(dplyr::all_of(full)) |>
  cor()
cor_range <- sprintf("%.3f", range(within_cor[upper.tri(within_cor)]))
names_cy <- readr::read_csv("../cases/eu-frames/data/EUframes_cy.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::distinct(cntry, country)
tips_pre <- series |>
  datawizard::data_filter(measure == "es_1574_tips", year < 2009) |>
  dplyr::distinct(cntry) |>
  dplyr::left_join(names_cy, by = "cntry") |>
  dplyr::pull(country) |>
  sort()
```

This module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd) is about where the data that social scientists analyse are held, and how a researcher gets hold of them. The Eurobarometer waves of the EU-frames case come from the GESIS archive under an account and terms of use that forbid passing them on, the economic series of its panel come from the World Bank and Eurostat, and the files of SCORE and Multi100, the two projects that checked the claim, sit on the Open Science Framework (OSF). Section 1 sets out the three kinds of route by which data are reached, section 2 maps the sources that hold most of the quantitative data of sociology, political science and demography, section 3 follows the data of the case from their sources to a file on your disk, programmatically where the source allows it and by hand where it does not, and section 4 is about citing what you downloaded.

The routes are taught where the course needs them. The session on repositories and data sources on the first day of the [Extended course](../tracks/eu-frames-extended/day-1.qmd) reads this module, and the participants of that course download the raw files of the case before it starts, by the route that section 3.1 describes, for the work on respondents of its third day, from a file of respondents that each participant builds at the end of the second day, as the [data management module](data-management.qmd) shows. The self-study track downloads the Eurobarometer waves by the same route in [stage 3](../tracks/self-study/stage-3.qmd). The one-day workshop downloads nothing, because the workspace and the browser lab of the case hold its data, and there section 3 explains where those files came from. The [repositories module](repositories.qmd) covers the other side of the exchange, where a finished piece of work is deposited so that others can find it.

Two things are outside the scope of this page. Qualitative data archives are not discussed, although the UK Data Service, which appears in the tables below, and the Qualitative Data Repository both hold qualitative collections. And nothing here replaces the terms of use of a particular dataset, which change, and which you read before you download.

## 1. Three ways in {#sec-access}

Almost every dataset on this page is reached by one of three routes, and the vocabulary of the archives follows them.

**Open download.** The file is on a public page or behind a public API (an interface through which a program, rather than a person at a browser, asks a server for data), under a licence that permits reuse with attribution, typically Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY), a dedication to the public domain such as CC0, or an open government licence. World Bank indicators, the aggregate tables published by Eurostat, the public-use files of the US statistical agencies and most replication packages in political science are of this kind. Nothing is asked of you except the citation and, for official surveys, respect for the rules that protect the respondents.

**Registration and licence.** You create an account under your own name, agree to conditions (no redistribution, no attempt to identify anyone, citation of the source, sometimes non-commercial use), and download. This is the standard route for survey microdata, meaning files with one row per respondent: the European Social Survey, the Eurobarometer at GESIS, the safeguarded collection of the UK Data Service, SHARE, IPUMS. The registration is free, immediate or nearly so, and the archive keeps a record of who took what.

**Application and secure access.** The data are too detailed to leave the archive: linked administrative records, fine geography, exact dates of birth, business microdata. You apply with a project description, your institution may have to be recognised as a research entity, you may have to complete a training course and become an accredited researcher, and you then work either on a scientific-use file sent under contract or inside a secure environment where nothing leaves without being checked. Examples are the microdata held by Eurostat, the controlled collection of the UK Data Service through SecureLab, the Secure Research Service of the Office for National Statistics and the contract route of the German Socio-Economic Panel. Allow weeks or months.

Two distinctions run across all three. **Microdata against aggregates:** a respondent-level file needs the second or third route, while the country-year or region-year tables computed from it are usually open. The EU-frames panel of the course is of that kind, an open aggregate built from licensed microdata. And **catalogue against archive:** a catalogue such as the CESSDA Data Catalogue or re3data tells you that a dataset exists and where it is held, and the archive that holds it is where you register and download.

The EU-frames case takes the second route. Its data, sixteen waves of the Standard Eurobarometer, are held by GESIS and downloaded by hand after a registration, under terms of use that forbid passing the files on, so the course ships country-year aggregates only, under CC BY 4.0.

## 2. The map {#sec-map}

The tables name the source, what it holds, how it is reached and where to start. 'Open' means the first route above, 'registration' the second and 'application' the third; the note says what the registration or application involves where that is not obvious. They are a starting point for a question of your own rather than a census of the field.

### 2.1 Cross-national survey programmes {#sec-surveys}

| Source | What it holds | Access | Where to start |
|---|---|---|---|
| **European Social Survey (ESS)** | Attitudes, values and behaviour across Europe every two years since 2002; eleven rounds at the time of writing, plus the CRONOS online panels | Registration, free; the survey describes its data as "freely accessible data for academics, policymakers, civil society and the wider public" | [ESS Data Portal](https://ess.sikt.no/en/), which searches, builds a custom file and downloads |
| **Eurobarometer** | Surveys run twice a year for the European Commission since 1974, with the Standard, Special and Flash series; the source of the EU-frames case | Registration with GESIS, free for academic use, one study per wave | [GESIS Eurobarometer Data Service](https://www.gesis.org/en/eurobarometer-data-service) and [search.gesis.org](https://search.gesis.org/); [section 3.1](#sec-gesis) |
| **European Values Study (EVS) and World Values Survey (WVS)** | Values and beliefs in waves since 1981; the two are harmonised into a joint file for the 2017 wave | Registration, free; EVS is distributed by GESIS, WVS from its own site | [europeanvaluesstudy.eu](https://europeanvaluesstudy.eu/), [worldvaluessurvey.org](https://www.worldvaluessurvey.org/) |
| **International Social Survey Programme (ISSP)** | One themed module a year since 1985, repeated on a cycle (role of government, social inequality, religion, work) across some forty countries | Registration with GESIS, free | [issp.org](https://issp.org/), files via search.gesis.org |
| **SHARE** | The Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe: a longitudinal panel of people over fifty, with linked administrative records for several countries | Registration, "free of charge for scientific use globally", under published conditions of use | [share-eric.eu](https://share-eric.eu/) |
| **Generations and Gender Programme (GGP)** | Longitudinal surveys on family, fertility and partnership | Registration | [ggp-i.org](https://www.ggp-i.org/) |
| **Comparative Study of Electoral Systems (CSES)** | Post-election surveys harmonised across countries, with system-level variables | Open | [cses.org](https://www.cses.org/) |
| **OECD PISA and PIAAC** | Student assessment (PISA) and adult skills (PIAAC) microdata, with contextual questionnaires | Open download of the public-use files | [PISA databases](https://www.oecd.org/en/data/datasets/pisa-2022-database.html), [PIAAC](https://www.oecd.org/en/about/programmes/piaac.html) |
| **The regional barometers** | Afrobarometer, Latinobarómetro and the Arab Barometer: repeated public-opinion surveys on their continents | Registration or open, by barometer | [afrobarometer.org](https://www.afrobarometer.org/), [latinobarometro.org](https://www.latinobarometro.org/), [arabbarometer.org](https://www.arabbarometer.org/) |

### 2.2 Archives and catalogues {#sec-archives}

| Source | What it holds | Access | Where to start |
|---|---|---|---|
| **UK Data Service (UKDS)** | The national collection for the UK: the large government surveys, the household panels and cohorts, the census aggregates, ESRC-funded project data, and the international series it distributes. Its three tiers are named "Open" (download without registration), "Safeguarded" (registration and the End User Licence, sometimes a Special Licence with a use statement) and "Controlled" (SecureLab, for accredited researchers whose organisation signs an agreement) | By tier; registration is open to UK academic users through their institution and to others through a separate route | [ukdataservice.ac.uk](https://ukdataservice.ac.uk/), [types of data access](https://ukdataservice.ac.uk/help/access-policy/types-of-data-access/) |
| **GESIS Data Archive** | Germany's central social-science archive and the distributor of the Eurobarometer, EVS, ISSP, ALLBUS and the European Election Studies; each study is assigned an access category from free download to depositor permission, and the archive runs a Secure Data Center for the sensitive files | Registration, free; category by study | [search.gesis.org](https://search.gesis.org/) |
| **CESSDA Data Catalogue** | The joint catalogue of the European social-science archives (the UK Data Service, GESIS, DANS, Sikt, the Finnish Social Science Data Archive and their peers), searchable in one place; downloads happen at the archive that holds the study | Catalogue open; access by archive | [datacatalogue.cessda.eu](https://datacatalogue.cessda.eu/) |
| **ICPSR** | The Inter-university Consortium for Political and Social Research at Michigan, the largest social-science archive in the United States; a part of the collection is public, most of it is for members, and restricted files are applied for | Institutional membership for most files; check whether your university is a member | [icpsr.umich.edu](https://www.icpsr.umich.edu/) |
| **Harvard Dataverse** | An open repository run on the Dataverse software, holding tens of thousands of datasets deposited by researchers and journals, including much replication material from political science | Open, with terms set per dataset; a public API, and the `dataverse` R package | [dataverse.harvard.edu](https://dataverse.harvard.edu/) |
| **re3data** | The registry of research data repositories, for finding out which repository holds a kind of data at all | Open | [re3data.org](https://www.re3data.org/) |

### 2.3 Household panels and cohorts {#sec-panels}

| Source | What it holds | Access | Where to start |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Understanding Society** (and the British Household Panel Survey before it) | The UK household longitudinal study, some forty thousand households followed yearly since 2009, with the BHPS back to 1991 | Safeguarded at the UK Data Service; the linked and geographic files need a Special Licence or SecureLab | [understandingsociety.ac.uk](https://www.understandingsociety.ac.uk/) |
| **The UK birth cohorts** | The 1946, 1958, 1970 and Millennium cohorts and their successors, coordinated by CLOSER | Safeguarded at the UK Data Service | [closer.ac.uk](https://www.closer.ac.uk/) |
| **German Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP)** | The German household panel since 1984, at the DIW Research Data Center | Application: a data distribution contract, free for scientific use | [DIW SOEP](https://www.diw.de/en/diw_01.c.678568.en/research_data_center_soep.html) |

### 2.4 Official statistics and administrative data {#sec-official}

| Source | What it holds | Access | Where to start |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Eurostat, the database** | The aggregate statistics of the EU: unemployment, GDP, population, migration, living conditions, by country and region and year, behind a public API | Open | [ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database); the `eurostat` R package |
| **Eurostat, the microdata** | Fourteen collections of respondent-level files, among them the EU Labour Force Survey, EU-SILC (income and living conditions), the Household Budget Survey, the Adult Education Survey and the European Health Interview Survey | Application: the institution must be recognised as a research entity (about four weeks), then a research proposal (about eight to ten weeks); scientific-use files are sent, secure-use files are worked in the Safe Centre or at accredited access points, and the files are destroyed at the end of the project | [Eurostat microdata](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/microdata) |
| **Office for National Statistics (ONS)** | The UK's official statistics, open on the site and through an API; the detailed microdata through the Secure Research Service | Open for the published tables; accredited researcher status for the Secure Research Service | [ons.gov.uk](https://www.ons.gov.uk/) |
| **National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS)** | The national health surveys of the United States, among them the National Survey of Family Growth: public-use files of every cycle, with their setup files, codebooks and user guides | Open, without registration, under the data use restrictions of NCHS; restricted variables only through the NCHS Research Data Center | [cdc.gov/nchs/nsfg](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nsfg/index.htm) |
| **IPUMS International** | Harmonised census microdata: "104 countries – 656 censuses and surveys – over 1 billion person records", with the US and other IPUMS collections beside it | Registration, free, with approval of a stated purpose; the `ipumsr` R package fetches extracts | [international.ipums.org](https://international.ipums.org/) |
| **ADR UK** | Administrative Data Research UK: linked government records for research, worked in secure settings by accredited researchers | Application and accreditation | [adruk.org](https://www.adruk.org/) |

### 2.5 Indicators from the international organisations {#sec-indicators}

| Source | What it holds | Access | Where to start |
|---|---|---|---|
| **World Bank Open Data** | The World Development Indicators and the other Bank databases, by country and year, under CC BY 4.0; the source of the macro variables of the EU-frames case | Open; a public API, and the `WDI` and `wbstats` R packages | [data.worldbank.org](https://data.worldbank.org/); [section 3.2](#sec-worldbank) |
| **OECD Data Explorer** | Statistics published by the OECD on its members and partners, behind an SDMX API | Open; the `OECD` and `rsdmx` R packages | [data-explorer.oecd.org](https://data-explorer.oecd.org/) |
| **ILOSTAT** | Labour statistics, including the modelled unemployment estimates that the World Bank republishes | Open; the `Rilostat` R package | [ilostat.ilo.org](https://ilostat.ilo.org/) |
| **Our World in Data** | Curated and documented compilations of the above, with the sources traced | Open | [ourworldindata.org](https://ourworldindata.org/) |

### 2.6 Political and institutional datasets {#sec-political}

| Source | What it holds | Access | Where to start |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem)** | Expert-coded measures of democracy for every country since 1789 | Open; the `vdemdata` package is on GitHub rather than CRAN | [v-dem.net](https://v-dem.net/) |
| **Manifesto Project** | Coded party election programmes since 1945 | Registration and an API key; the `manifestoR` R package | [manifesto-project.wzb.eu](https://manifesto-project.wzb.eu/) |
| **ParlGov** | Parties, elections and cabinets in the established democracies | Open | [parlgov.org](https://www.parlgov.org/) |
| **Party Facts** | A crosswalk that links the party codes of many datasets, the ESS among them, to one another | Open | [partyfacts.herokuapp.com](https://partyfacts.herokuapp.com/) |
| **Chapel Hill Expert Survey (CHES)** | Expert placements of European parties on policy dimensions | Open | [chesdata.eu](https://www.chesdata.eu/) |
| **Quality of Government (QoG)** | Country-year compilations of governance indicators from many sources | Open | [Quality of Government Institute](https://www.gu.se/en/quality-government) |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Pick a question you have worked on, or would like to. Find a dataset that could answer it in two of the catalogues above, the CESSDA Data Catalogue and re3data, and write down for each: the archive that holds it, the access route, and the first step you would have to take on Monday morning. If the two catalogues disagree about where the data are, note the disagreement as well.
:::

## 3. The routes of the case {#sec-course}

The subsections run from the most restricted source to the most open: the GESIS archive, which holds the Eurobarometer waves, then the World Bank and Eurostat, from which the panel takes its country-level series, and the OSF, which holds the files of SCORE and Multi100. Each route is written as steps that you can follow from a fresh R session. Code that downloads is shown and not run on this page, which is built without a connection, and the results printed beside it come from the copies that the course keeps. None of it has to be done for the one-day workshop, where the data are already in place.

Every download in this section ends with a check that the file is the one that the course used. The simplest check is a checksum: the MD5 sum is a short code computed from the contents of a file, which changes if a single byte of the file changes, so two files with the same MD5 sum are the same file. `tools::md5sum()` computes it in R, and several of the sources publish it beside the file.

### 3.1 The GESIS archive: the Eurobarometer waves {#sec-gesis}

The outcomes of the EU-frames case are built from sixteen Eurobarometer waves between 2004 and 2013, the waves that included the question asking what the European Union means to the respondent personally, with its fourteen items. The files are distributed by **GESIS – Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences**, the German social-science archive, which describes itself as "[the largest German infrastructure institute for the social sciences](https://www.gesis.org/en/institute)" and which runs the Eurobarometer Data Service for the European Commission. In the words of the service, "Eurobarometer data and documentation can be downloaded free of charge from the GESIS Data Catalog", and "the data are available to the scientific community for research and education" ([Eurobarometer Data Service](https://www.gesis.org/en/eurobarometer-data-service)). Every step below was checked in a browser on 8 September 2026, and the file downloaded from GESIS at the end was byte for byte identical to the one from which the course panel was built. The participants of the [Extended course](../tracks/eu-frames-extended/before.qmd) download the sixteen files before the course, and the self-study track in [stage 3](../tracks/self-study/stage-3.qmd).

The sixteen studies are these. Every one is in the access category that GESIS labels "0 – Data and documents are released for everybody", which means a free account and nothing more; the file names are the ones that arrive in your download folder, and the two marked as zipped arrive as `.zip` archives that are unpacked by the course build script.

: The sixteen studies, with the versions current on 8 September 2026. GESIS re-releases files under new version numbers; the build script checks what you downloaded against this list.

The route is manual. Registration is a web form with a captcha, and every download asks for a purpose of use in your own name, so the steps below are clicked rather than scripted. A CRAN package, gesisdata (version 0.1.2, of July 2023), scripts the same clicks by driving a web browser through RSelenium, but it has not been updated since, and a report of a failed download, opened on its issue tracker in February 2025, has no answer, so the course does not rely on it.

**Before you start: two settings in the browser.** GESIS serves its pages in German by default and marks them as English, so Chrome quietly translates them into an English that differs slightly from the English version of the site, and the labels on your screen will not match the ones below. Turn translation off for the site (the translate icon in the address bar, then "Never translate this site") and click **English** in the page header. The sidebar then reads *Datasets / Questionnaires / Codebook* rather than *Datensätze / Fragebögen*.

![The catalogue as it first appears in a browser set to English: German, with the language switch at the top right.](../assets/gesis/00-german-default.jpg){.border}

**1. Register once, before the course.** Open [search.gesis.org](https://search.gesis.org/), click *Login* and then "You are not yet registered?". The form asks for your name, country, discipline, email and a password of at least eight characters with a capital letter, a number and a special character. There is one kind of account and no institutional check. The registration page states that "Registration at GESIS is free of charge, open to all". Registration is a web form with a captcha and cannot be scripted, which is why it should be done in the week before the course. One trap: the checkbox that says "I have read the GESIS Usage Regulations" links to the data-protection notice rather than the terms of use, which are at [gesis.org/en/institute/data-usage-terms](https://www.gesis.org/en/institute/data-usage-terms) and are summarised below.

![The registration form, upper half.](../assets/gesis/08-register-top.jpg){.border}

![The registration form, lower half, with the password rule and the two checkboxes.](../assets/gesis/09-register-bottom.jpg){.border}

**2. Find each study by its number.** Type the study number, `ZA4056`, into the search box and press Enter, and the search returns one hit. Do not search by wave name. "Eurobarometer 61.0" returns about nine hundred datasets with the 2023–2026 waves at the top and the one you want nowhere on the first page, and a `?q=` address pasted into the browser fills the box without running the search. The direct address `https://search.gesis.org/research_data/ZA4056` works too, and the table above links every study that way.

![Searching by wave name: nine hundred hits, the wanted study not among them.](../assets/gesis/01-search-wave-number.jpg){.border}

![Searching by study number: one hit.](../assets/gesis/02-search-za-number.jpg){.border}

**3. Read the study page.** It gives the title, the version, the DOI, the fieldwork dates and the countries, and, in the right-hand panel, three download links: *Datasets*, *Questionnaires* and *Codebook*. The questionnaires and the codebook download without an account; they are the documents that say which variable records which question in that wave, and the [data management module](data-management.qmd#sec-eu-frames) uses them.

![The study page of ZA4056, with the Downloads panel on the right.](../assets/gesis/03-study-page.jpg){.border}

**4. Download the Stata file.** Click *Datasets*. A dialog lists four files: an SPSS portable file, a syntax file defining missing values, the Stata file and the SPSS file. Take the Stata file only, the one ending in `.dta`. The course script reads that format with its labels, and the others are not needed. Above the list is a **Purpose of use** dropdown, in which you state a purpose in your own name. Choose "in the course of my studies" if you are a student, and "for further education and qualification" otherwise. The option "in a course as lecturer" is for the lecturer and not for participants. Signed out, the same click produces only a "Login required" box. Signed in, the file arrives under the name given in the table, with no further prompt.

![The download dialog, signed in, with the purpose-of-use dropdown and the four files.](../assets/gesis/04-download-datasets.jpg){.border}

![The same click when signed out.](../assets/gesis/07-login-required.jpg){.border}

**5. Put all sixteen in one folder** outside the workspace, and run the build script that the [data management module](data-management.qmd#sec-eu-frames) describes. It unpacks the two zipped studies, reads the sixteen files, checks each against the checksum of the file from which the course was built, and writes one respondent-level file into a folder that the workspace never commits.

**The terms you accepted.** The terms of use, valid since 4 February 2026, are the document to which every download dialog links, and four of their clauses shape how the course handles these files. Redistribution: "The provision of the database to third parties is not permitted", and third parties "include, but are not limited to, publishers, libraries, data archives, or research data repositories", so no respondent-level file goes into any repository, public or private. Identification: "The presentation or publication of individual cases, even if there is no direct reference to individuals, is not permitted", while "summary presentations of data, as is customary in scientific papers and lectures, are permitted", which is the line that separates the microdata from the aggregates distributed with this course. Citation: the DOI and the version number of each file must appear in anything published from them. The fourth clause bears on any course taught with AI assistants. It reads "The use of AI systems for processing the database provided to the user by GESIS is prohibited", with exceptions only on request. In practice that means the respondent file is never opened in a session that an AI assistant can read, never pasted into a chat, and never handed to an assistant that has access to the objects in your R session. The aggregates distributed with the course are not covered by this restriction. The terms also ask for deletion of the files at the end of the project, and put a contractual penalty of €10,000 on a breach of the redistribution and de-anonymisation clauses.

![The access categories, from the terms of use: the sixteen Eurobarometer studies are all in the first row.](../assets/gesis/06-access-categories.jpg){.border}

The terms permit the sharing of aggregates coarse enough that no respondent can be recovered, and those aggregates, released under their own licence, are all that this course shares from the Eurobarometer. The [data codebook](../cases/eu-frames/data/EUframes_cy_codebook.md) states that division in its licence section, CC BY 4.0 for the derived country-year panel, GESIS terms for everything beneath it. The rebuild for this course started from these sixteen files and averaged the respondents 'as interviewed', which is one of the choices offered among the measurement decisions of the specification menu. The [weights module](weighting.qmd) explains the alternative.

### 3.2 The macro indicators, at the World Bank {#sec-worldbank}

The EU-frames panel takes two of its country-level series from the World Development Indicators of the World Bank, released under its open licence (CC BY 4.0):

- `unemp`: unemployment as a percentage of the total labour force, the national estimate, indicator `SL.UEM.TOTL.NE.ZS`, which the Bank republishes from ILOSTAT;
- `growth`: annual GDP growth in percent, indicator `NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG`.

There are two ways to get a series. On the site, open [data.worldbank.org](https://data.worldbank.org/), search the indicator code, choose the countries and years and download a CSV. In R, the `WDI` package (version 2.8.0 on CRAN, released in August 2026) does the same in one call and returns a tidy country-year table:

```{r}
#| eval: false
macro <- WDI::WDI(
  country   = c("AT", "BE", "BG", "CY", "CZ", "DE", "DK", "EE", "ES", "FI", "FR", "GB",
                "GR", "HU", "IE", "IT", "LT", "LU", "LV", "MT", "NL", "PL", "PT", "RO",
                "SE", "SI", "SK"),
  indicator = c(unemp = "SL.UEM.TOTL.NE.ZS", growth = "NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG"),
  start = 2004, end = 2013
)
```

The Bank publishes other estimates of the same quantity, among them the ILO modelled estimate, and Eurostat publishes its own series, built from the EU Labour Force Survey and fetched from the Eurostat database. The next section sets out the series that the EU-frames case uses besides the two above, and why two of them are not on the curve of the claim.

The third macro variable of the EU-frames panel, `bailout`, is not downloaded at all. It is coded from the record of EU and IMF financial assistance programmes, country by country and year by year, and the codebook lists the programmes and years used. Many contextual variables enter a panel in this way, through a documented rule applied by hand, with the source of each fact stated.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Run the `WDI` call above in your workspace and compare its `unemp` column with the one in `EUframes_cy.csv` for one country. They should agree to the decimal for most country-years and differ for a few, because the Bank revises series after the fact. Write down which years differ and by how much. Any macro series can change between downloads in this way, which is why the codebook records the download date.
:::

### 3.3 The published series {#sec-series}

The specification menu of the EU-frames case offers more than one published series for each of the two economic measures, and the choice among them is a measurement decision, because the series measure one construct, the national unemployment rate or the growth of output, in slightly different ways. For unemployment there are five: the national estimate of the World Bank above (`wb_nat`), which is the series of the course panel and of the reanalyst C6HJR, and four series cut from the Eurostat tables that the other reanalysts merged. Those are the rate in the labour force aged 15–74 from the table `une_rt_a_h` (`es_1574_act`, the series of 018OL), the unemployed as a share of the whole population aged 20–64 from the same table (`es_2064_pop`, KQXUE), the rate in the labour force aged 25–64 from the Labour Force Survey table `lfsa_urgan` (`es_2564_lfs`, the annual counterpart of the quarterly series of PRL47), and the rate in the labour force aged 15–74 from the short table `tipsun20` (`es_1574_tips`, KEVF1). For growth there are two, the World Bank series and the national accounts of Eurostat in the table `nama_10_gdp` (`es_growth`). All seven are held for the 270 country-years in `cases/eu-frames/data/macro/predictor_measures.csv`, so that the workspace can merge them without a connection, and the Eurostat tables are kept in the source repository as they were retrieved.

The four unemployment series that cover all 270 country-years differ in age band and denominator, and the population-based series of KQXUE is a different quantity from a labour-force rate, but within countries they move together. Once the mean of each country and of each year is removed, they correlate with one another at between `r cor_range[1]` and `r cor_range[2]`, so all four stay on the curve, where the choice among them carries `r measure_share` of the variance of the claim-aligned partial correlations.

The other two series left the curve, because choosing either of them changes who is in the analysis as well as how the economy is measured. The table `tipsun20` has rows for `r coverage$cells[coverage$measure == "es_1574_tips"]` of the 270 country-years, in `r coverage$countries[coverage$measure == "es_1574_tips"]` countries, with none for the United Kingdom and, before 2009, rows for only `r paste(tips_pre, collapse = " and ")`. Choosing it therefore halves the panel and moves the question towards the crisis years: swapped into the `r tips$n_pairs` unemployment specifications of the curve, it leaves `r tips_below` of them below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, against `r curve_below` of the unemployment specifications on the curve itself, and it changes the class of `r tips_changes` of the pairs. It is a decision about the sample presented as one about the measure, which is why the [decision map](../cases/eu-frames/map.qmd) rewrites the population in the estimand statement when the series is chosen. The Eurostat growth series has no row for the United Kingdom, `r coverage$cells[coverage$measure == "es_growth"]` country-years in `r coverage$countries[coverage$measure == "es_growth"]` countries, which costs one country for the same reason, although within the countries that it covers it moves with the World Bank series and leaves the class of every one of its `r es_growth$n_pairs` pairs unchanged. Coverage of this kind is worth checking before any series is merged, since a merge that silently drops rows changes the population of the question without changing a line of the model.

### 3.4 The OSF: the files of SCORE and Multi100 {#sec-osf}

The Open Science Framework holds the dossier that SCORE kept on the paper and the components in which the Multi100 analysts left their materials, and the [repositories module](repositories.qmd#sec-score-dossiers) reads that dossier as a record. A public file on the OSF needs no account: every file has a short address of five characters, and `https://osf.io/download/` followed by that address returns the file itself. The `osfr` package (version 0.2.9 on CRAN, of September 2022; its development continues on GitHub under rOpenSci) reaches the same files through the API of the OSF and lists the contents of a project or a component. The case takes one file from the OSF, the course panel, `EUframes_cy.csv` in the main folder of [osf.io/6zqct](https://osf.io/6zqct/), the fork of the Multi100 record of analyst C6HJR that the facilitator maintains. The workspace script `R/get_data.R` fetches it with osfr as an exercise, and falls back to the committed copy when the network or the OSF is down.

A checksum is computed from the bytes of a file, so a program that rewrites the ends of the lines of a text file changes it without changing a single value; git on Windows does that to CSV files unless it is told otherwise, which is why a value-by-value comparison, as in the [data management module](data-management.qmd#sec-reproduce), is the safer check of a text file that has passed through a repository.

The OSF itself is changing. From 19 February 2027 every OSF project becomes read-only, so these files will still download at the same addresses indefinitely, but no project will receive new ones. The maintained copy of the EU-frames panel from then on is the [`replication-lab`](https://github.com/CodeMoreh/replication-lab) repository on GitHub, and the [repositories module](repositories.qmd#sec-osf) sets out what the change means for depositing your own work.

## 4. Citing data {#sec-citing}

A dataset is cited like a publication, with the producer, the title, the version or wave, the distributor and the persistent identifier, and most archives print the citation that they want on the study page. The archives of the map ask for it in different forms:

- **The Harvard Dataverse** prints a citation for every dataset, with its version and a **UNF**, a checksum that Dataverse computes from the values in the data rather than from the bytes of the file, so that the same data saved in another format give the same UNF.
- **The ESS** gives a citation for each data file, with its edition and DOI, and asks that a modified file be cited as "Adapted from ESS Round X, version number X".
- **NCHS** gives no DOI to the NSFG files, so a citation names the agency, the survey, the cycle and the file, with the date of download.
- **GESIS** asks for the study number, the DOI and the version of each wave, which the table of section 3.1 gives for the sixteen of the EU-frames case.
- **The World Bank** asks for the indicator and the date of access.

Two further habits help a reader who wants to repeat your analysis. Record the date on which you downloaded a series, because the World Bank and Eurostat revise past years without renaming the file, and a reader who repeats your download a year later will get slightly different numbers. And keep the version identifier of a survey file, because the ESS, SHARE, the NSFG and the Eurobarometer all release corrected editions of the same round.

## Sources {#sec-sources}

The access rules of the map were read from the pages of the archives themselves on 8 September 2026: the [types of data access](https://ukdataservice.ac.uk/help/access-policy/types-of-data-access/) page of the UK Data Service, which names the Open, Safeguarded and Controlled tiers, the End User Licence, the Special Licence and SecureLab; the [microdata pages of Eurostat](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/microdata), which describe research-entity recognition, the proposal step, scientific-use and secure-use files; the [SHARE data access page](https://share-eric.eu/data/data-access); the [IPUMS International](https://international.ipums.org/) front page, from which the coverage figures are quoted; and the [ESS Data Portal](https://ess.sikt.no/en/). The GESIS pages (the terms of use with their access categories, the Eurobarometer Data Service page, the registration form and the study pages) were read in a browser on the same day, as [section 3.1](#sec-gesis) describes. The ICPSR pages could not be read by the tools used to prepare this module, so the description of ICPSR in the table above rests on the long-standing arrangements of the archive and should be checked against its current pages before you rely on it.
